title: Given items with weights and values and a capacity, maximise total value when you may take fractions of items. Explain why a greedy by value-to-weight ratio is optimal here, contrast it with 0/1 Knapsack, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort items by value-to-weight ratio descending and fill greedily, splitting the last item if it only partly fits.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fractional Knapsack** – a variant of the knapsack problem where items may be taken in fractions, not just whole.
- **Value density** – the value-to-weight ratio `value / weight` measures how much return each unit of capacity delivers.
- **Greedy strategy** – sort items by density descending, take each whole while capacity remains, and take a fraction of the last item that only partly fits.
- **Optimality proof** – because partial selection is allowed, skipping a denser item in favour of a sparser one can never help, so a simple exchange argument proves the greedy is optimal.
- **Complexity** – O(n log n) for sorting, O(n) for the greedy scan, giving O(n log n) overall with O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a fixed capital pool of 50 crore to deploy across investment opportunities. Each opportunity has a different return-per-crore ratio. Because the bank can fund any opportunity partially, it ranks them by return-per-crore, funds the best ones fully, and invests whatever capital remains into a fraction of the next-best opportunity. This is exactly the fractional knapsack strategy.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Fractional Knapsack is the problem where a greedy strategy is not just a heuristic but provably optimal, and the reason is the single word fractional. Because you are allowed to take a partial amount of any item, you compute each item's value-to-weight ratio, sort items from densest to least dense, and fill the capacity from the top of that list. You take each item whole while it fits, and when you reach an item that only partly fits, you take exactly the fraction that fills the remaining capacity and add a proportional share of its value.

The contrast with 0/1 Knapsack is the point interviewers probe. In the 0/1 version items are indivisible, so greedy by ratio can be wrong: a small dense item might leave leftover capacity that a larger item could have filled more valuably. The moment fractions are permitted, that trap disappears because any leftover capacity can always be filled with a slice of the next-densest item, and a simple exchange argument proves the ratio-sorted greedy optimal.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to deploy a fixed 50-crore capital pool across investment opportunities that could be funded partially. He ranked opportunities by return-per-crore, funded the top ones fully, and invested the remaining capital as a fraction of the next-best opportunity. Using BigDecimal for all money calculations ensured that rounding errors did not creep into the fractional computation.

The cost is dominated by the sort at O(n log n), and the greedy scan itself is O(n). For a banking portfolio service handling thousands of opportunities, this runs in real time. The senior-level insight is that the fractional knapsack is the LP relaxation of the 0/1 integer knapsack, which is why solvers use it as an upper bound in branch-and-bound.

Remember one sentence: Fractional Knapsack sorts by value-to-weight ratio and fills greedily, and it is provably optimal because fractions eliminate the all-or-nothing obstacle that makes 0/1 Knapsack need dynamic programming.

---

keyPoints: Compute value-to-weight ratio (density) for each item and sort descending.
Take each item whole while capacity remains, then take a fraction of the last item.
Greedy is provably optimal for fractional knapsack via an exchange argument.
0/1 Knapsack defeats greedy because items are indivisible and requires DP.
Time complexity is O(n log n) for sorting, O(n) for the greedy scan.
Fractional knapsack is the LP relaxation of the 0/1 integer knapsack.
